article.title: Vehicle Transport Decisions
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The cheapest quote usually looks like the obvious choice at first glance. It’s always the lowest number that wins the booking. When it does, the client misses their chance of checking whether the experience goes smoothly. After all, price tag is what blinds us from vetting a provider that offers a great quality service. It’s just sad that many transport bookers realize that too late. Open Versus Enclosed Transport This decision affects more than cost, though it does affect cost greatly. Open transport, the standard car-carrier trucks you see hauling multiple vehicles on public roads, exposes cars to weather, road debris, and dust for the entire journey. It’s fine for most vehicles making a standard move. For anything with sentimental or genuine financial value beyond the ordinary- a classic car, a recent luxury purchase, a vehicle with a factory paint finish you don’t want touched by road grit, enclosed transport removes that exposure entirely. It costs more, sometimes 30 to 50 percent above open transport rates, but the vehicle arrives in exactly the condition it left in. Choosing based purely on the lower open-transport quote is how people end up disappointed by minor paint chips or a layer of grime that a car wash won’t fully remove. Door-to-Door Versus Terminal-to-Terminal Pickup Some vehicle transport services offer door-to-door pickup and delivery, where the truck comes to your actual address at both ends. Others operate terminal-to-terminal. This means that you drop the car at a depot and collect it from a depot at the destination. The savings from this method are real, which may reach up to several hundred dollars on a long interstate trip. What doesn’t get mentioned as clearly is the added logistics on your end. Here, you’d have to arrange transport to and from depots that might not be conveniently located. As such, you end up storing the vehicle at a terminal for a day or two if pickup timing doesn’t align with your schedule. For someone with flexible time, terminal transport makes sense. But for someone who sees this as a conflict with their commitments, this is just added noise to an already busy day. How the Company Handles Delays and Rescheduling Every long-distance transport job carries some risk of delay. It’s just like how you can still be late at work despite leaving home early. Weather or mechanical issues with the carrier come into play. Don’t forget traffic. How the company updates its clients and adjusts when they encounter delays is what saves you from worries. A company willing to explain their process for handling delays before you book gives you a glimpse of a possible good handler. Ask this question directly during the quoting process, and pay attention to how specifically they answer it. Vague reassurances like “we’ll sort it out” mean less than a company that can describe an actual process, because a genuine process suggests they’ve dealt with delays enough times to have a system for managing them properly. Insurance Coverage Limits and Exclusions The cheapest quote sometimes comes with inadequate insurance coverage. Don’t forget the saying, “you get what you pay for.” If the policy only gives low cargo coverage and a ridiculously high excess, you’re actually not holding onto anything. This leaves you exposed when they total your car or damage it with a repair amount that’s under the excess. Comparing quotes while disregarding the coverage means comparing incomplete numbers, so don’t bother. A quote that’s $150 cheaper but covers your vehicle for only 10% of its actual value is going to war bare-handed.
